newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West Coast crude edges up in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West Coast crude edges up in quiet trade.

text.p: U.S. West Coast light crude prices inched up Monday with broader market gains while trade remained subdued because of August pipeline scheduling.
"It's the end of the month and scheduling is being done, and people are starting to get ready for September," said a Los Angeles refinery trader.
Regional benchmark Alaska North Slope (ANS) crude, which last traded in the West Coast market in mid-June at $2.16 under benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing, didn't trade Monday.
September spot WTI was nearly unchanged Monday, up one cent to $19.69/19.74 a barrel.
Traders said the main ANS seller, BP Oil, kept trying to sell at a $1.85 discount to WTI, but buyers declined the price due to large amounts of South American and Mexican crude available.
With five cargoes of Maya (Mexican) crude scheduled for delivery during July and August, and four Oriente's (Ecuador) running in plants, ANS has remained in low demand, buyers said.
Traders said both grades would remain in demand during September.
"Oriente will still be a crude that will be looked at and Maya will certainly be too," the trader said.
Loreto (Peru) crude could also run, traders said.

Separately, Arco said it had space to run all crude shipments requested by shippers on its Line 63 pipeline during August. The Line was often prorationed since a January 1994 earthquake shut a companion line.
Line 63 runs between California's San Joaquin Valley (SJV) oil fields and Los Angeles refineries.
